title: Interferometric Quantum Polynomial Chaos Expansion as a Generative Model for Calorimeter Shower Simulation
authors: Jamal Slim, Saverio Monaco, Florian Rehm, Dirk Kruecker, Frank Gaede, Kerstin Borras
abstract: We present the quantum polynomial chaos expansion, a generative algorithm in which a single circuit is the entire model, and we use it to learn calorimeter images. In a classical chaos expansion the randomness is the input and the coefficients are fitted. Here the randomness is still the only input, entering the circuit as rotation angles and re-uploaded at every block, so that each measured observable is a chaos expansion of the latent variables whose order equals the circuit depth, and what is fitted are the gate angles themselves. Expressivity therefore grows with depth rather than with classical coefficients, correlations between outputs arise only from entangling gates, and a single latent wire read by all qubits carries the collective mode of the data. Nothing fitted stands between the circuit and the sample, so switching the entanglers off is a setting of the model itself and provably yields independent outputs, and attribution of the learned correlations to individual gates becomes a measurement. Choosing between two measurement bases shot by shot sharpens attribution into certification, and the trained model violates the Bell bound obeyed by every classical generative model with local response, whatever its size. We train the model on Geant4 shower data, execute the identical circuit on a superconducting processor with its accuracy loss predicted in advance, prove a no-go theorem for the tail dependence of every smooth generator read out through expectation values, and identify the circuit primitive that removes this limit.
summary: This paper introduces an Interferometric Quantum Polynomial Chaos Expansion (QPCE) as a novel generative model for simulating particle calorimeter showers. By encoding the simulation into a quantum circuit, it leverages the depth of the circuit rather than classical coefficients to capture complex statistical dependencies. This approach allows the model to reproduce subtle structural features of real detector data that are inaccessible to standard classical generative models.
main_problem: The primary goal is developing a fast, accurate generative model for simulating high-energy physics calorimeter showers, which are computationally intensive using traditional methods.
main_result: The proposed Interferometric Quantum Polynomial Chaos Expansion (QPCE) successfully models the complex dependence structure of shower data, reproducing non-trivial structural properties like tail asymmetry that classical models cannot capture.
method: It employs a quantum circuit as a generative model, where randomness enters via rotation angles. The training involves minimizing an energy distance between generated and target distributions using adjoint gradients.
model_or_system: The system is the simulation of particle showers in calorimeters. The model is the QPCE, which uses a single quantum circuit whose depth dictates the order of the chaos expansion for latent variables.
key_observables: Tail asymmetry ($\lambda_L - \lambda_U$), mean absolute correlation $|ho_S|$, and structural properties like rank statistics ($D$).
important_parameters: Circuit depth ($L$) acts as the truncation order; training uses L-BFGS optimization.
main_assumptions: The method assumes that the circuit structure itself can encode complex, non-classical correlations necessary for accurate simulation.
figures_summary: Figures compare structural correlation measures (Spearman rank) and tail behavior ($\Lambda$) between Geant4 data, QPCE simulations, and actual hardware measurements.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the QPCE framework by contrasting it with classical PCE. It details the circuit ansatz, describes the training/generation/verification pipeline, presents results showing structural fidelity on both simulated and physical hardware, and concludes by discussing the model's inherent advantages in attribution.
why_interesting: While focused on HEP, the core methodology—using quantum circuits to encode complex statistical dependencies (chaos expansion) for generative modeling—is highly relevant to simulating non-equilibrium dynamics or complex many-body states where classical sampling fails.
